prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks operating at the 10^-18 level of accuracy and stability

statement.case_for: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes Doppler and recoil effects for neutral atoms while cancelling the light shift to first order, and Ye's group then drove strontium lattice clocks to 10^-18 systematic uncertainty and into the regime where many-body effects matter. Both steps rest on atomic-structure physics that I can judge directly: the magic wavelength depends on polarisabilities that can be calculated and measured, and the blackbody-radiation shift is the dominant systematic. The result is concrete and reproduced by several independent laboratories, with clock comparisons across institutes. It enables tests of relativistic redshift at millimetre scales, searches for varying constants and dark matter, and a pending redefinition of the second. The credit is clean with two names, and the prize is distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize for control of single trapped quantum systems. It gets the largest opening support in this shortlist alongside B013 (two first places, five top-three placements), but I rest the case on the physics, not on the count.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap and framing. Hall and Haensch were recognised in 2005 for the comb that makes optical clocks readable, and Wineland in 2012 for the ion control that produced the other leading clock family, so a sceptic can call lattice clocks a successor engineering advance and not a new discovery. The redefinition of the second has not happened, so the practical culmination is still pending. Credit also extends beyond two people: Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, PTB and SYRTE groups and the ion-clock community all contributed, and any two-name split leaves some of them out. If the committee wants a prize that opens a new field of physics and not a new level of measurement, B013 is the stronger candidate on that criterion.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first because a theoretical prediction was followed by experiments in which nature delivered correlated insulators and superconductivity, and he ranks the lattice clock second while noting the overlap with the Hall, Haensch and Wineland prizes.
responses.response: I agree that B013 is the more field-opening discovery and I ranked it second myself. I still place the clock first, for two reasons. First, the clock's maturity is clearer: every claim of 10^-18 performance has been checked in independent laboratories, while for magic-angle graphene the pairing mechanism and the nature of the correlated states are unsettled, and I hear that as a real caution about timing and not a footnote. Second, the B013 credit set is contested in a way the clock's is not: Cao and Fatemi, who carried the 2018 experiments, are outside the supplied names, and so are the earlier twisted-bilayer theorists. I accept that a more conceptual committee could reasonably reverse our order, and I would not oppose B013 if the credit question can be settled.

responses.point: Johansson ranks the Cirac-Zoller theory first as the blueprint for physical quantum information processing, and ranks the lattice clock sixth, on the view that the clock's metrology is less original than a conceptual blueprint.
responses.response: I put B034 third and share your view that its attribution is the cleanest on the list: two decisive theorists, and decades of confirmation on several platforms. Where I differ is on how much it is separable from what was recognised in 2012. Much of the demonstrated payoff, the gates and the simulators, came through the experimental work of Wineland, Blatt, Monroe and others, so a theory-only prize about ion gates would look partly like a second prize for the same story. I do not think the clock has that problem to the same degree, because lattice clocks are a different platform and a different physical idea. I would call B034 the best fallback, not the lead, and I note that you also point out that the cold-atom simulation half of the citation would need narrower wording.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks the geometric-phase discovery first as exceptional conceptual work that underlies much of modern physics, and ranks the lattice clock fifth, noting that the Hall and Haensch prize and Wineland's recognition cover neighbouring ground.
responses.response: I agree that Aharonov-Bohm and Berry are conceptually deep, and I do not dismiss the argument that foundational ideas are underrecognised. My difficulty with B008 is a fair-credit one, and you raise it yourself: the two effects are distinct discoveries 25 years apart, Bohm is dead, and Ehrenberg-Siday and Pancharatnam have priority claims, so a joint citation would honour a lineage and not a single result. On the clocks, I take the overlap point seriously but read it differently: the 2005 prize recognised the comb and the earlier spectroscopy, not the lattice-clock idea, and Wineland's prize concerned ions, whose clock performance has been matched and then surpassed by neutral-atom lattices. I would accept that framing risk and write the citation narrowly on lattice clocks.

responses.point: Kroll shares first place for the lattice clock and calls it a decisive, lasting result from the laser-spectroscopy tradition, while disclosing a personal link to the Hall laboratory tradition from which the field descends.
responses.response: I agree on the substance and on the two-name configuration, and I thank you for the disclosure about the Hall tradition. Because we agree, I want to test it. If your link to that tradition and my field proximity both bias us toward an AMO prize, the committee should check B061 against B013 on the same criteria and not just count that two of us ranked it first. I would also ask you whether you see any case for adding a third name, since I do not: the credited set already contains the two people whose contributions were decisive.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges lattice clocks as a distinct discovery or as a continuation of the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should come first, or whether the 10^-18 demonstrations already suffice.
How to weigh the credit of other lattice-clock groups (Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and the PTB and SYRTE teams) against a two-name prize.
Whether B013 is ripe: the credit question (Cao, Fatemi, earlier twisted-bilayer theorists) and the unresolved mechanism of superconductivity both bear on a decision this year.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with B061 is apparent from my profile: I have no documented collaboration with Katori or Ye, though I work in a neighbouring area of atomic structure. My documented collaborations (L'Huillier, Keller, Dahlstrom, Argenti, Schuch, Indelicato) involve attosecond physics, storage-ring work and highly charged ions, none of which are on this shortlist. I note only a general field proximity to the atomic and precision-measurement candidates (B061, B034, B005), and Indelicato's exotic-atom and QED work is loosely adjacent to B005.
